name: Sweet William
summary: A biennial or short-lived perennial commonly grown as a bedding and cut flower. Species-level sources describe clustered flowers and seed propagation; cultivars and flower colors vary, so none is assigned here.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Dianthus barbatus L. NC State and RHS describe Sweet William as the common horticultural name. This record is species-level and does not identify a named color or cultivar series.

growth.short: Biennial or short-lived perennial with dense flower clusters
growth.guidance: RHS describes a biennial or short-lived perennial with rosettes and upright flowering stems, often 40–60 cm in its profile; NC State gives a regional species range of 1–2 feet. Retain this variation rather than asserting a cultivar-specific size.

cultivation.short: Sun to partial shade; well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: RHS recommends full sun and well-drained neutral to slightly acidic soil. NC State notes partial shade can be useful in hot summer climates and describes loamy, slightly alkaline conditions. These are regional garden recommendations, not hydroponic specifications.

care.short: Deadhead as needed; watch for moisture-related disease
care.guidance: RHS says deadheading may be done as required and lists possible slug, aphid, mildew, rust, virus, and Fusarium problems. NC State also flags crown rot in poorly drained soils. Susceptibility is not assigned to any unnamed cultivar.

harvestUse.short: Grown for ornamental borders and cut flowers
harvestUse.guidance: RHS lists cut flowers, bedding, and borders among suitable garden uses. This profile makes no edible-use claim.

problems.short: Poor drainage can contribute to crown rot
problems.guidance: NC State identifies crown rot in poorly drained soils and notes rust and slugs/snails as potential problems; RHS lists additional possible pests and diseases. These are reported risks, not a diagnosis or cultivar-level resistance statement.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The cited sources describe ornamental soil/container growing and do not establish hydroponic performance.

evidence.note: RHS describes a leaf rosette and stiff, erect flowering stems.

height.reason: Regional species sources give differing ranges; no standardized cultivar or growing context is identified.

spread.reason: No consistent species-level spread is established across the selected sources.

spacing.reason: RHS seedbed spacing is not an indoor container or Garden pod capacity recommendation.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not converted into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Hollyhock
summary: A tall ornamental biennial-to-short-lived perennial grown for its flowering spikes. Seed-raised plants often flower in a later season; height and disease response vary among unnamed types.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Alcea rosea L. and records Althaea rosea as a synonym. NC State calls it hollyhock and notes biennial-to-annual garden behavior. No named cultivar or color is assigned.

growth.guidance: NC State reports 5–8 feet height and 1–2 feet width for its regional species account and notes that the plant readily reseeds. Iowa State describes many hollyhocks as flowering the summer after sowing. Cultivar and climate can alter life cycle and stature.

cultivation.short: Full sun and moist, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun to light shade and moist, well-drained soil; UC ANR's Master Gardener fact sheet describes full sun and careful root handling when transplanting. Regional advice is not a hydroponic compatibility claim.

care.short: Leave room for air movement and keep foliage dry when watering
care.guidance: University of Wisconsin Extension advises avoiding dense planting to improve air circulation and watering at soil level to reduce leaf wetness associated with rust management. Do not assume a resistant cultivar: resistance is incomplete and varies by rust variant.

harvestUse.short: Primarily ornamental; flowers are used in garden displays
harvestUse.guidance: NC State and Illinois Extension describe hollyhock as an ornamental and cutting-garden/background plant. This profile does not claim the plant is safe to eat.

problems.short: Hollyhock rust can cause spotting, stunting and leaf loss
problems.guidance: UW-Madison Extension describes orange-yellow spots on lower leaves and raised brown to dark-red pustules on leaf undersides; infection can stunt plants and cause premature leaf drop. Some varieties resist some variants but are not reliably resistant to all.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected sources address garden soil and do not establish hydroponic cultivation.

evidence.note: NC State describes rigid, towering flowering spikes.
NC State reports 5–8 ft for its regional species profile; converted to rounded centimeters and not assigned to an unspecified cultivar.

name: Common Foxglove
summary: A biennial or short-lived perennial ornamental with a first-year leaf rosette and a tall second-year flower spike. All parts are toxic if ingested; keep away from children and pets and avoid using it as food or medicine.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Digitalis purpurea L. in Plantaginaceae. The record is for common foxglove species, not a named series such as Camelot, Dalmatian, or Foxy.

growth.short: First-year rosette followed by a flowering spike
growth.guidance: UW-Madison Extension describes a low rosette in the first year and a typically 3–4-foot flowering spike in the second. It notes that some named varieties flower in year one, but that behavior is not attributed to this unnamed species-level entry.

cultivation.short: Full sun to light shade; moist, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: UW-Madison Extension recommends full sun to light shade and light, moist soil high in organic matter; NC State notes afternoon shade and moist, well-drained soil. These garden conditions are not hydroponic specifications.

care.short: Manage self-seeding and handle with care
care.guidance: UW-Madison Extension notes abundant seed production and recommends deadheading when excess seedlings are undesirable; allow some seed to mature if maintaining a self-sustaining planting. Wear gloves if skin is sensitive and prevent ingestion; all parts are toxic.

harvestUse.short: Ornamental and cut flower only; not for consumption
harvestUse.guidance: UW-Madison Extension describes its use as an ornamental and cut flower. Both Wisconsin and NC State sources warn that all plant parts are toxic if ingested. Do not present historical medicinal use as a safe use recommendation.

problems.short: Ingestion is highly toxic; powdery mildew and aphids may occur
problems.guidance: NC State flags high-severity poisoning characteristics and lists fungal disease and insect problems. UW-Madison Extension states all parts are toxic if ingested and notes possible powdery mildew and aphids. Keep plant material away from children and pets.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Ornamental garden culture does not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: The source describes a basal rosette and upright second-year flower spike.

height.reason: The species varies by site and cultivar; the UW source's spike range is not a universal mature plant height.

spread.reason: No consistent cultivar-independent spread is established.

spacing.reason: Landscape thinning guidance does not establish container or indoor system capacity.

light.reason: Outdoor sun/shade guidance is not converted to an indoor grow-light category.

name: Annual Baby's Breath
summary: A seed-grown annual with airy flower clusters, used in cottage and cutting gardens. It is distinct from perennial baby's breath Gypsophila paniculata; the two species should not share life-cycle or cultivation claims.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO recognizes Gypsophila elegans M.Bieb.; NC State describes it as annual baby's breath and distinguishes it from the perennial florist species. No cultivar is assigned.

growth.short: Annual, quickly growing and airy in form
growth.guidance: NC State describes annual plants about 1–2 feet tall and 1.5–2 feet wide, with wiry stems and open flower clusters. Those dimensions are a species-level regional description, not a container guarantee.

cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and moist, sandy loam, while noting adaptation to other well-drained soils and partial shade with reduced flowering. Avoid overly wet conditions; no hydroponic method is established by this source.

care.guidance: NC State suggests successive sowings every 3–4 weeks until July to extend the bloom season. It also warns that the species may escape cultivation; monitor self-seeding and local status.

harvestUse.guidance: NC State lists the species as suitable for cut and dried flowers and describes it as an airy ornamental. Do not transfer florist-use claims about perennial G. paniculata without separate evidence.

problems.short: Wet conditions may contribute to stem or root rot
problems.guidance: NC State lists stem and root rot especially in overly wet conditions, as well as aphids, slugs, and snails; it also notes potential escape into the wild. These are species-level cautions, not a cultivar resistance assessment.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected Extension source describes garden soil culture and does not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: NC State describes airy clusters on wiry stems and an erect annual habit.
